resources.string: Edible, toxic and their look-alikes, side by side
Never eat a mushroom identified with this atlas: have your harvest checked by a pharmacist or a mycological society.
Keep a sample and a photo of what was eaten.
An atlas for learning to compare, not to identify: ANSES, the French food-safety agency, advises against recognition apps, which are wrong too often.

Look-alikes are chosen mostly from the confusions actually seen in France by poison centres (ANSES), not from intuition. Among the edible species, some were added because pickers often bring them to be checked (Basel-Stadt cantonal laboratory, reports for 2022, 2024 and 2025).
Each status is cross-checked between health authorities, official texts, medical journals and encyclopedias. When sources disagree, the most cautious status wins. Last check: October 2026.
Drawings are original diagrams made from published descriptions. Colours and proportions are typical; in nature they vary a lot. Sizes are approximate.

• Pick only mushrooms you know perfectly, whole, neither too young nor too old.
• Photograph the harvest before cooking it.
• Never eat them raw: 20 to 30 minutes in a pan, or 15 minutes in boiling water (water discarded).
• Keep them cold and eat them within two days.
• Use a basket rather than a plastic bag.
• Do not give them to young children.
• Symptoms after a meal: call a poison centre and mention the meal, even after more than 12 hours.
The sources could not be loaded.
The works cited by these articles (Bresinsky and Besl, Michelot and Toth, Flammer, Eyssartier and Roux, Clowez and Moreau…) are known only through them.
Once commonly eaten, until the Second World War. A mycologist dies of it in 1944; the immune mechanism is described in 1985.
Once sold in markets and thought good. Twelve cases of muscle breakdown published in 2001, three of them fatal. Sale suspended in France in 2004, then banned: it is no longer eaten.
Once eaten after boiling. Sale banned in France since 1991; now ranked deadly.
Judged poisonous in 1821, sometimes given as edible before 1999. Today: not worth eating rather than dangerous.

Long cited as a middling edible. In 2015 ANSES judged it can cause digestive trouble, even after long cooking; a 2016 order suspended the sale of fresh honey fungus without a notice about full cooking.

Listed in several guides as a mediocre edible. In 2015 ANSES judged that it can cause digestive upset, even after cooking; a 2016 decree suspends the sale of fresh granulated bolete without a note on thorough cooking.

Sometimes eaten, and even judged edible in Eastern Europe. In 2015 ANSES judged that the risk cannot be ruled out, even after cooking; a 2016 decree suspends the sale of fresh olive brittlegill without a note on thorough cooking.

string-array.name: myco_g_chanterelle_points
string-array.item: Chanterelle: thick, forked ridges like veins. Jack-o’-lantern: real, thin, crowded gills.
The chanterelle comes out of the ground. The jack-o’-lantern grows in a clump on wood, a stump or roots.
Chanterelle: apricot smell, cream-white flesh. Jack-o’-lantern: oily smell, orange inside the stem.
False chanterelle: thin, crowded, regularly forked gills that peel off with a fingernail. No apricot.

string-array.name: myco_g_boletus_points
string-array.item: Porcini: fine white net at the top of the stem. Bitter bolete: coarse, dark brown net.
Porcini: pores white, then yellow-green. Bitter bolete: pink pores. Satan’s bolete: red pores.
Porcini: white flesh that does not change. Satan’s bolete: flesh that turns blue.
The bitter bolete is not toxic, but its bitterness ruins everything. Satan’s bolete makes you ill.

string-array.name: myco_g_parasol_points
string-array.item: Parasol: large (over 10 cm), stem banded with brown, double ring that slides, no volva.
Death cap: sac-like volva at the base, hanging ring, olive-streaked stem, olive-green cap.
Panther cap: white warts on a brown cap, sharp-edged bulb, smooth ring.
Small lepiotas (under 10 cm): deadly, never to be picked.

string-array.name: myco_g_field_points
string-array.item: Field mushroom: gills pink, then chocolate brown. White amanitas: gills always white, sac-like volva.
Yellow stainer: yellows when rubbed, bulb at the base, ink or phenol smell, wide ring.
Field mushroom: spindle-shaped stem with no bulb, thin fleeting ring.
In 2022, two deaths after a deadly amanita was taken for a field mushroom or a fallow-field agaric.

string-array.name: myco_g_morel_points
string-array.item: Morel: honeycomb cap. False morel: rounded folds like a brain.
Cut lengthwise: the morel is hollow in a single cavity, cap joined to the stem at its base.
False morel: chambered inside, cap joined to the stem at several points.
The morel is always eaten cooked. The false morel may not be sold in France.

string-array.name: myco_g_amanita_points
string-array.item: Blusher: flesh and gills turn red when damaged. Panther cap: white flesh that never changes.
Blusher: ring striate on top. Panther cap: smooth ring.
Panther cap: sharp-edged bulb topped with rings; pure white warts on dark brown, striate margin.
Fly agaric: red cap, white gills and stem. Washed by rain, it resembles the Caesar’s mushroom, whose gills and stem are yellow.

string-array.name: myco_g_oronge_points
string-array.item: Caesar’s mushroom: yellow gills and stem. Fly agaric: white gills and stem.
Caesar’s mushroom: large white sac-like volva, always present. Fly agaric: bulbous base with rims, no sac.
Caesar’s mushroom: smooth cap, striate margin. Fly agaric: white warts, washed off by rain, leaving a paler cap.
At the egg stage Caesar’s mushroom has none of these marks: do not pick it.

string-array.name: myco_g_stgeorge_points
string-array.item: St George’s: white gills, white spores. Red-staining inocybe: conical cap that turns red, gills that brown, tobacco-brown spores.
Livid pinkgill: gills yellowish then pink, pink spores, and a floury smell too: the smell is not enough.
St George’s: appears in spring. Pinkgill: mostly autumn, but sometimes from summer.
The inocybe causes sweating and salivation; the pinkgill, vomiting and heavy diarrhoea.

string-array.name: myco_g_fairyring_points
string-array.item: Fairy ring champignon: widely spaced gills, cap with an umbo. Fool’s funnel: close gills, frosted cap, often dished.
Both grow on lawns, sometimes in fairy rings.
Fairy ring champignon: smell of cut hay, sometimes cyanide. Fool’s funnel: floury smell.
The deadly brown roll-rim is also mistaken for it: strongly rolled margin, decurrent gills that brown.

string-array.name: myco_g_entoloma_points
string-array.item: Livid pinkgill: notched gills, butter-yellow then pink. Clouded agaric: pale, close gills.
Clouded agaric: stout, light grey stem, grey cap with a white bloom. Pinkgill: white to cream stem, often club-shaped.
Both smell floury: the smell is not enough.
The clouded agaric can upset the digestion; the livid pinkgill causes severe gastroenteritis.

resources.string: Shaggy ink cap, or common ink cap?

string-array.name: myco_g_inkcap_points
string-array.item: Shaggy: cylindrical white cap covered in upturned fibres. Common: egg-shaped, grey, pleated cap.
Both melt into black ink, starting from the gills.
Common ink cap: no alcohol during the meal or in the 72 hours after.
Shaggy: safe with alcohol, but eat it young and fast, white when cut.

string-array.name: myco_g_woodtuft_points
string-array.item: Woodtuft: the cap dries from the centre outward, pleasant smell. Funeral bell, deadly: from the rim inward, floury smell.
Scales below the ring are not enough: the funeral bell can have some too.
Sulphur tuft: sulphur yellow, gills yellow then green, very bitter. Toxic.
Honey fungus: also in tufts on stumps and roots; ANSES links it to digestive trouble, even after cooking.

string-array.name: myco_g_greenforms_points
string-array.item: Death cap: ring and sac-like volva, smooth cap, free white gills. Green-cracking russula: no ring, no volva, cap cracked into patches.
Russula: gills and flesh snap like chalk. Death cap: fibrous flesh that does not snap.
Yellow knight: yellow gills and stem, no ring, no volva; it is no longer eaten.
The green form of the death cap is mistaken for a russula or a green tricholoma.

string-array.name: myco_g_whiteforms_points
string-array.item: Destroying angel: fragile ring and sac-like volva, white gills. Dove-coloured tricholoma: no ring, no volva, floury-smelling flesh.
Livid pinkgill: pale grey, very fibrous cap, yellow then pink gills, pink spores. Dove-coloured tricholoma: white gills, white spores.
Wood mushroom: pale cream then pink then chocolate-brown gills, aniseed smell, very wide ring. Amanitas have always-white gills and a volva.
The volva is underground: only whole mushrooms are picked.
The floury smell is found in both the dove-coloured tricholoma and the livid pinkgill: it is not enough.

string-array.name: myco_g_clitopilus_points
string-array.item: Miller: decurrent gills, white then pink, pink spores. Fool’s funnel: whitish to cream gills, white spores.
Miller: strong smell of fresh flour. Fool’s funnel: a less floury smell.
White clitocybes contain muscarine: sweating and salivation from a few minutes to 2 hours after the meal.
The spore print settles it: let the spores fall on a sheet of paper before concluding.

string-array.name: myco_g_redpore_points
string-array.item: Dotted-stem bolete: yellow stem covered in red dots, no net. Satan’s bolete: stem with a fine net.
Dotted-stem: dark brown, velvety cap. Satan: whitish, chalky, very large cap.
Scarlet-stemmed bolete: yellow pores, stem yellow above and red below with a white net; bitter, toxic.
Both turn blue: deep navy for the dotted-stem, pale blue for Satan’s.
Dotted-stem: cook at least 20 minutes. Satan’s and scarlet-stemmed: toxic, digestive upset.
ANSES records Satan’s boletes and scarlet-stemmed boletes picked instead of dotted-stem boletes.

string-array.name: myco_g_milkcap_points
string-array.item: Saffron milk cap: orange milk. Woolly milkcap: white, acrid milk.
Saffron milk cap: orange cap, concentric zones, pitted stem. Woolly milkcap: pink and ochre cap, hairy margin.
Cut the mushroom to see the milk before concluding: once the colour of the milk is noted, the confusion is no longer possible.
The woolly milkcap irritates the gut: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea.

string-array.name: myco_g_puffball_points
string-array.item: Puffball: pure white, solid and even inside, with pearly spines. Amanita egg: smooth, with a cap and a stem already inside.
Earthball: thick skin, inside grey then violet-black marbled with white, sour smell.
Cut it in two lengthwise: it is the only way to see what is inside.
The young, egg-shaped forms of the death cap are mistaken for puffballs.

string-array.name: myco_g_greyknights_points
string-array.item: Tiger: silvery cap covered in scales in circles, thick stem, floury smell. Grey knight: mouse-grey, fibrous cap, smaller, no floury smell.
Tiger: chalky soil, at altitude, mostly summer and autumn. Grey knight: mostly under pines.
The tiger is toxic, even in small amounts: violent vomiting, 24 to 48 hours.
The grey knight is debated: not recommended. The Swiss controllers say it is easily mistaken for the tiger and for some fibrecaps.
Livid entoloma: gills that turn pink, pink spores. The grey tricholomas have whitish to grey gills and white spores. ANSES records livid entolomas picked instead of « petits gris » (grey knights).

string-array.name: myco_g_laccaria_points
string-array.item: Amethyst deceiver: dark, matt violet, gills of the same colour and distant, fibrous and hard stem. Lilac bonnet: pink to violet or grey, whitish to pinkish gills, fragile and hollow stem.
Lilac bonnet: striate margin, clear smell and taste of radish. The deceiver has no radish smell.
The lilac bonnet contains muscarine: sweating, salivation, nausea.
The deceiver can accumulate arsenic on polluted soil.
ANSES records mycenas picked by people looking for amethyst deceivers.

string-array.name: myco_g_shaggy_points
string-array.item: Parasol: banded stem, double sliding ring, flesh that does not change. Chlorophyllum brunneum: smooth stem, single ring, flesh that reddens.
Chlorophyllum rhacodes (shaggy parasol): smooth grey stem, rounded bulb, double ring, flesh that turns bright red when cut.
Chlorophyllum brunneum: large bulb with a sharp edge, often off-centre; it grows near houses, in gardens and on compost heaps.
Chlorophyllum brunneum causes digestive upset, rarely serious; C. rhacodes is good but poorly tolerated by some.
Small lepiotas (under 10 cm): deadly, never to be picked.

string-array.name: myco_g_monkhead_points
string-array.item: Trooping funnel: large (7 to 20 cm), cream to buff, deeply decurrent gills, solid fibrous stem, white spores.
Livid entoloma: notched gills that turn pink, floury smell, pink spores.
The miller is also edible, but its spores are pink.
ANSES records livid entolomas picked instead of trooping funnels.

resources.string: White flesh, yellow under the skin
Tawny cap, paling as it dries
Yellow and red stem, net at the top

string-array.name: myco_phalloides_traits
string-array.item: Olive-green to yellowish cap, 5 to 15 cm, paler toward the edge
White gills that stay white
Skirt-like ring under the cap
White sac-like volva at the base, hidden in the soil: it can be missing if slugs ate it
White stem, finely streaked with olive
Smell sweet at first, then sickly · white spores
Under oaks, beeches, chestnuts… from late summer to autumn

resources.string: Deadly. Signs come late, more than 6 hours after the meal, when the liver is already hit. Neither cooking, drying nor freezing destroys the toxin, and a young one is already toxic. About 30 g, half a cap, can be enough.

string-array.name: myco_virosa_traits
string-array.item: Entirely white, gills included
Conical to domed cap, often irregular, up to 8–10 cm
Slender, shaggy or downy stem, 10 to 15 cm
Fragile white ring, often torn
Sac-like volva at the base
Mostly under conifers, sometimes birches · summer to late autumn

resources.string: Deadly: same toxin as the death cap. A single medium specimen can be enough. A white mushroom is never “safe”.

string-array.name: myco_muscaria_traits
string-array.item: Bright red cap, 8 to 20 cm, covered with white warts
After rain the warts wash off and the red fades
White gills and stem
White skirt-like ring
Bulbous base with one or two rings of rims, no sac-like volva
Under birches and conifers · autumn

resources.string: Toxic: confusion, hallucinations, nausea, 30 to 90 minutes after the meal, sometimes convulsions. Rarely fatal, but hospital care may be needed. Washed by rain, it resembles the Caesar’s mushroom, whose gills and stem are yellow.

string-array.name: myco_pantherina_traits
string-array.item: Brown to blackish-brown cap, 4 to 15 cm, small pure white warts
Striate cap margin
White gills
White ring, smooth (no streaks)
Sharp-edged bulb topped with one or two rings
White flesh that does not change colour
Under beeches and other broadleaves, or conifers · late summer to autumn

resources.string: Toxic, more than the fly agaric: same toxins, more concentrated. Violent digestive upset, confusion, convulsions especially in children. In 2022 this kind of poisoning made up 21.6% of severe cases in France (ANSES). It is sometimes taken for the parasol or the blusher.

string-array.name: myco_rubescens_traits
string-array.item: Pinkish-brown to wine-coloured cap, 4 to 15 cm, covered with dirty grey flakes
Flesh and gills turn red when damaged (sometimes little in dry weather)
White ring, striate on top
Swollen base without a volva, often eaten by larvae
White gills · white spores

resources.string: Edible only when well cooked: raw, it is toxic (a haemolysin destroyed by heat). Easily confused with the panther cap, which is toxic.

string-array.name: myco_edulis_traits
string-array.item: Brown cap, 4 to 20 cm, smooth, paler at the margin
Pores white, then yellow, then olive green
Massive, bulbous stem with a fine white net, mostly on the upper half
White flesh that does not change colour when cut, mild taste
Olive-brown spores
Under broadleaves and conifers · summer to autumn

resources.string: No net, flesh that turns blue or grey, red pores: it is not a porcini. Firm young ones only, always cooked.

string-array.name: myco_felleus_traits
string-array.item: Light to dark brown cap, 4 to 15 cm
Pores white at first, then dirty pink, browning when pressed
Stem marked with a dark brown, thick, raised net
White flesh that does not change, very bitter
Pink-brown spores
Mostly under oaks and beeches

resources.string: Inedible: the bitterness, made worse by cooking, ruins a whole dish. May cause vomiting. It contains a little muscarine, at doses judged too low to be dangerous.

string-array.name: myco_satanas_traits
string-array.item: Whitish to grey cap, up to 25 cm
Pores yellow-orange then blood red, turning blue when touched
Obese stem, yellow at the top, bright red below, with a fine net
Whitish flesh that slowly turns blue when cut
Weak smell when young, rotten meat in old ones
Oaks, beeches, chalky soils, warm regions · summer

resources.string: Toxic: vomiting, sometimes bloody diarrhoea, especially raw or undercooked. Rarely fatal in a healthy adult, but violent. In 2022 it was the second most frequent toxic species found in French harvests (ANSES).

string-array.name: myco_cibarius_traits
string-array.item: Egg yellow, 4 to 10 cm, funnel-shaped, wavy margin
Underside with thick, forked, strongly decurrent ridges: no real gills
Fruity apricot smell
Cream-white, firm flesh
Grows from the ground under broadleaves or conifers, never on wood
Pale yellow spores · summer to late autumn

resources.string: Several close species, such as the pale chanterelle, are also edible. Frequent confusion with the toxic jack-o’-lantern: it was one of the most common in 2024 (ANSES).

string-array.name: myco_olearius_traits
string-array.item: Bright orange to coppery, 6 to 14 cm, funnel-shaped
Underside with real, thin, crowded, decurrent, unforked gills
Grows in clumps on wood, stumps or roots of broadleaves
Orange flesh, even inside the stem
Oily smell · gills faintly glow in the dark
Southern France and the Mediterranean, moving north

resources.string: Toxic: nausea, vomiting, heavy diarrhoea, cramps, risk of dehydration. Among toxic harvests identified in 2022, 8.5% contained it (ANSES).

string-array.name: myco_aurantiaca_traits
string-array.item: Orange, 3 to 8 cm, velvety cap, darker centre
Thin, crowded gills, regularly forked, that peel off with a fingernail
Slender stem, darkening to blackish toward the base
Soft, orange-yellow flesh, no apricot smell
Under conifers, on rotting wood or humus

resources.string: Not worth eating: soft flesh, sometimes poorly tolerated. The poisonings once blamed on it mostly came from confusion, notably with the jack-o’-lantern.
The Swedish mycologist Elias Fries called it “poisonous” in 1821; before 1999, guides sometimes gave it as edible. Today it is judged not worth eating rather than dangerous.

string-array.name: myco_procera_traits
string-array.item: Large: parasol-shaped cap up to 25 cm with a smooth brown umbo at the centre
Brown shaggy scales on a pale ground
Stem 10 to 30 cm, banded with brown on a cream ground, bulbous
Thick double ring that slides along the stem
No volva · white free gills · white spores
Meadows, clearings, open woods · July to October

resources.string: Only the cap is eaten: the stem is tough. Never a lepiota under 10 cm. In France it is confused with the death cap, the panther cap, the livid entoloma and poisonous lepiotas (ANSES).

string-array.name: myco_brunneoincarnata_traits
string-array.item: Small: cap only 3 to 4 cm, pinkish-brown scales on a pale ground
One large, darker scale at the centre
Stem 2 to 3.5 cm: pink above, covered with brown scales below, split by a dark ring zone
White free gills · flesh reddens when cut
Lawns, parks, gardens · warm regions

resources.string: Deadly: same toxins as the death cap. About 100 g can severely damage the liver. It grows on lawns, where it is taken for a small parasol; signs come late, more than 6 hours after the meal.

string-array.name: myco_campestris_traits
string-array.item: White cap, 4 to 10 cm, finely fibrous
Gills pink, then chocolate brown: never white
Thin, fleeting ring, often gone
Short spindle-shaped stem, no bulb or volva
White flesh that barely pinkens, does not yellow · pleasant button-mushroom smell
Meadows and pastures · late summer to autumn

resources.string: Edible, provided you do not make a mistake: in 2022 two people died after taking a deadly amanita for a field mushroom or a fallow-field agaric (ANSES). The gills of every specimen must be pink or brown, never white.

string-array.name: myco_xanthodermus_traits
string-array.item: White cap, cube- or cup-shaped at first, then flat, 6 to 15 cm
Yellows quickly when rubbed, especially at the cap edge and stem
Bulbous stem base, chrome-yellow flesh when cut
Wide, persistent ring, woolly underneath
Smell of ink, iodine or phenol, stronger when cooked
Gills pink then blackish brown, like the field mushroom
Meadows, edges, parks, gardens · July to November

resources.string: Toxic: vomiting and digestive upset. In 2022 it was the toxic species most often found in French harvests (25.7%, ANSES). The yellowing can be weak or absent.

string-array.name: myco_morchella_traits
string-array.item: Egg-shaped honeycomb cap of 4 to 10 cm, straw yellow to honey brown
Hollow in a single cavity, from the top of the cap to the foot
Cap joined to the stem at its base
Whitish, hollow, granular stem, sometimes flared
Spring (March to May): orchards, ash trees, woodland edges

resources.string: Toxic raw or undercooked: always cook it well. Cut in half lengthwise, it is hollow in a single cavity; if not, it may be a false morel.

string-array.name: myco_gyromitra_traits
string-array.item: Cap in folded lobes like a brain, reddish brown to chestnut, 3 to 11 cm
Cut lengthwise: chambered inside, cap joined to the stem at several points
Short, stocky stem, white to cream, furrowed
Brittle flesh, strong smell
Under conifers, acid or sandy soils · March to June

resources.string: Deadly: gyromitrin turns into methylhydrazine, which attacks the liver and the nervous system. Sale banned in France since 1991. Cooking fumes are also dangerous, and boiling does not remove everything.

Long eaten after boiling (its name, esculenta, means “edible”). Unpredictable poisonings, over a hundred fatal cases in the literature, then a suspected cumulative toxicity got it ranked as deadly. Its sale has been banned in France since 1991, as well as in Germany and Switzerland; it is still allowed in Finland, with warnings.

string-array.name: myco_paxillus_traits
string-array.item: Olive-brown to yellow-brown cap, 4 to 12 cm, felty, dipped into a funnel
Strongly rolled margin that stays rolled for a long time
Yellow-brown, decurrent, forked gills that peel off easily and brown when touched
Short stem, tapering toward the base, no ring
Yellowish flesh, no milk (unlike milk caps)
Under birches, lawns, damp ground · late summer to autumn · brown spores

resources.string: Deadly, without warning: after repeated meals, sometimes over years with no problem at all, the body makes antibodies that destroy its own red blood cells. Anaemia, kidney failure, sometimes death. No antidote. In France it is picked by mistake instead of the fairy-ring mushroom (ANSES).

It was commonly eaten in central and eastern Europe until the Second World War. In 1944 the German mycologist Julius Schäffer died after eating it. In 1985 the Swiss physician René Flammer described the immune mechanism. Guides only clearly warned against eating it around 1990; it is still eaten in Poland, Russia and Ukraine, where people die of it every year.

string-array.name: myco_equestre_traits
string-array.item: Bright yellow to olive-yellow cap, 5 to 10 cm, scaly orange-brown centre, a little sticky
Lemon to sulphur-yellow gills, crowded
Yellow, stocky stem with no ring or volva
White flesh, yellow under the skin, weak smell, mild taste
Sandy pine woods (Landes), autumn to winter · whitish spores

resources.string: Toxic: it breaks down muscle fibres (rhabdomyolysis). Unusual tiredness, hip and shoulder pain, sweating, dark urine, 1 to 3 days after several meals. Twelve cases in France between 1992 and 2000, three of them fatal. Sale banned in France.

Once highly prized, sold in markets and cooked as a salmis in the Landes. In 2001 doctors published twelve cases of muscle breakdown after repeated meals, three of them deaths. In 2004 France suspended its sale, then made the ban permanent in 2005, for the whole group T. equestre, T. auratum and T. flavovirens. The toxin is still unidentified.

string-array.name: myco_caesarea_traits
string-array.item: Bright orange-red cap, 8 to 20 cm, smooth, no warts; clearly striate margin, golden yellow
Golden-yellow gills, free, close
Yellow, solid stem with a wide, hanging ring, striate on top
Thick white volva, a large sac at the base: it is always present
White flesh, yellow under the cap skin · mild smell and taste · white spores
Under oaks, chestnuts, beeches, in warm places · July to November

resources.string: A prized edible, but only when identified with certainty. At the egg stage none of its features show and it looks like other amanitas, including the deadly death cap: serious poisonings have followed the picking of amanitas at that stage. Washed by rain, the fly agaric looks like it. Protected in several European countries.

string-array.name: myco_sinuatum_traits
string-array.item: Pale grey to yellowish-beige cap, 3 to 20 cm, convex then flat, not striate
Butter-yellow gills (rarely white), turning pinkish with age, notched around the stem
White to cream stem, fleshy, often club-shaped, no ring
White flesh, floury smell and taste, often unpleasant
Pink spores
Edges and open deciduous woods, mostly on chalky soil · mid-summer to late autumn

resources.string: Toxic: nausea, vomiting and heavy diarrhoea, with moderate liver damage. The Belgian poison centre gives 3 to 8 hours after the meal, other sources as early as 30 minutes; recovery takes 5 to 6 days and hospital is sometimes needed. The toxin is unidentified. The first signs look like death cap poisoning: without leftovers, diagnosis is difficult. In 2022, 8.5% of toxic pickings in France contained it (ANSES).

string-array.name: myco_nebularis_traits
string-array.item: Grey to grey-brown cap, 5 to 25 cm, often with a white bloom when young, rolled margin
Pale, close gills, often forked, up to slightly decurrent
Light grey stem, stout, swollen at the base
White, very thick flesh · strong smell, from floury to rancid
Pale yellow spores
Under broadleaves and conifers · autumn

resources.string: Not recommended: even a small portion can upset the digestion of some people. It is mistaken for the livid pinkgill, which is toxic, and whose gills turn pink.

string-array.name: myco_gambosa_traits
string-array.item: White-beige to pale apricot cap, 5 to 10 cm, matt and slightly velvety, rolled margin
White to cream gills, very close
Short, stocky stem, whitish, faintly striate
Thick white flesh · strong smell and taste of fresh flour
White spores
Meadows, hedges, orchards, often in rings · late April to June

resources.string: Edible, a spring mushroom. Two toxic look-alikes appear in the same season: the red-staining inocybe, with a conical cap that turns red, and sometimes the livid pinkgill, with gills yellowish at first then pink. The spore print is white; tobacco-brown for the inocybe, pink for the pinkgill. The floury smell is not enough: the pinkgill has it too.

string-array.name: myco_erubescens_traits
string-array.item: Conical to bell-shaped cap with an umbo, 3 to 7 cm, fibrous, margin often split
White to straw-yellow cap, then vermilion-brown
Close gills, white then ochre, staining red
Cylindrical, striate white stem that stains red · no ring
Tobacco-brown spores
Under broadleaves, mostly beeches · spring and summer

resources.string: Toxic: it contains muscarine, which causes, within minutes to 2 hours, sweating, salivation, tears, runny nose, breathing difficulty and a slow heart. Recovery usually comes in under 24 hours; atropine is sometimes needed (Belgian poison centre). Out in spring, it is mistaken for St George’s mushroom: this one turns red, the other does not.

string-array.name: myco_oreades_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2 to 6 cm, buff to reddish tan, paling as it dries; bell-shaped at first, then flat with a lasting umbo; grooved margin
Cream-white gills, thick, widely spaced
Slender stem, paler than the cap, hollow, elastic and very tough: it twists as it dries
Thin flesh · smell of cut hay, sometimes faintly of cyanide
White spores
Lawns, meadows, path edges, in arcs or fairy rings · spring to autumn

resources.string: A well-liked edible; the tough stem is thrown away (the Belgian poison centre advises it too). Toxic white clitocybes grow on the same lawns, sometimes in rings too: their gills are close, those of the fairy ring champignon widely spaced. The deadly brown roll-rim is also picked by mistake in its place in France (ANSES).

string-array.name: myco_rivulosa_traits
string-array.item: White to cream cap, 2 to 6 cm, frosted, often dished, sometimes cracked in circles; rolled margin
Close gills, whitish then cream
Short, fibrous, silky white stem, no ring
Floury smell
Meadows, lawns, parks, path edges, sometimes in fairy rings · summer to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: muscarine causes sweating, salivation, tears, vomiting and a slow heart, from a few minutes to 2 hours after the meal. Recovery usually comes in under 24 hours; atropine is sometimes needed. It can be fatal for a frail person. It grows on lawns, where children and pets play.

string-array.name: myco_atramentaria_traits
string-array.item: Egg-shaped cap, 3 to 7 cm, grey to grey-brown, pleated, opening little
Very close, free gills: white, then grey, then black
The cap melts into black ink starting from the gills
White to grey stem, long, smooth, hollow; ring absent or invisible
Blackish spores
Gardens, path edges, buried stumps, in tufts · summer to late autumn

resources.string: Edible, but never with alcohol: coprine blocks the breakdown of alcohol. A glass of wine or beer during the meal, or up to 72 hours after, causes flushing of the face and neck, headache, dizziness, sweating, vomiting and a drop in blood pressure. The effects pass within a few hours (Belgian poison centre).

string-array.name: myco_comatus_traits
string-array.item: White cylindrical cap, 6 to 12 cm tall, covered in upturned fibres, brownish at the top
Free gills, white, then pink, then black
The cap melts into black ink, less than the common ink cap
White cylindrical stem, swollen at the base, with a movable ring
Blackish spores
Lawns, grassland, path edges, rich soil, in groups

resources.string: Edible when young, while the gills are still white: eat it quickly, and throw away anything turning pink or black. Unlike the common ink cap, it is safe to eat with alcohol.

string-array.name: myco_galerina_traits
string-array.item: Small convex cap, 3 to 5 cm, brown to tawny, paling as it dries
Brownish gills, then tawny · rusty-brown spores
Stem 2 to 6 cm with a small fragile ring, clear on young ones, often gone later
Stem white and powdery above the ring, brown and silky below
Floury smell
On rotting wood, mostly conifer, alone or in small groups · summer to autumn

resources.string: Deadly: the same amatoxins as the death cap. The first signs come about twelve hours after the meal on average, up to 48 hours, like gastroenteritis; then the liver is hit. Intensive care, sometimes a liver transplant. It looks like the sheathed woodtuft and the sulphur tuft (Belgian poison centre).

string-array.name: myco_mutabilis_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 8 cm, shiny: honey to reddish-brown when damp, with a paler centre; cinnamon when dry
Yellowish or cinnamon gills, then ochre-brown
Stem up to 8 cm, smooth above the ring, scaly and darker below
Light, sagging ring that often disappears
Rusty spores · pleasant smell, mild taste
In tufts of sometimes fused stems, on broadleaf stumps · late spring to autumn

resources.string: A good edible, except the fibrous stem. But the deadly funeral bell can fool even experienced pickers. The woodtuft dries from the centre outward, the funeral bell from the rim inward; one smells pleasant, the other floury. The scales below the ring are not enough: the funeral bell can have some too.

string-array.name: myco_fasciculare_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 7 cm, sulphur yellow, darker orange-brown centre
Close gills, yellowish then greenish, brown when ripe
Curved, sulphur-yellow stem; no ring, only a fleeting veil remnant
Thin, sulphur-yellow flesh · very bitter taste
Purple-brown spores
In tufts fused at the base, on stumps and wood of broadleaves or conifers · spring to autumn

resources.string: Toxic: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, sometimes only 5 to 10 hours after the meal; it usually passes in a few days. One death from fulminant hepatitis is cited, but the dish contained other mushrooms. It resembles the funeral bell and the sheathed woodtuft (Belgian poison centre).

string-array.name: myco_mellea_traits
string-array.item: Cap 1 to 15 cm, light yellow, mustard or olive-brown, with fine dark fibres mostly at the centre
Gills white then yellowish, sometimes stained brown
Slender stem, striate above a white ring, flecked white below; fibrous and tough with age
White flesh, slightly bitter taste · white spores
In tufts, sometimes dozens of stems, on stumps, roots and trunks, mostly of broadleaves
Very common in autumn

resources.string: Not recommended: ANSES considers it can cause digestive trouble (diarrhoea, vomiting, pain) a few hours after the meal, and nothing shows that long cooking or canning removes the risk. Between 1999 and 2015, French poison centres recorded 83 cases. Some authors call it edible when young and well cooked. It grows in tufts like toxic look-alikes, the funeral bell and the sulphur tuft.

Long cited as a middling edible, sometimes only when young, it is judged indigestible and sometimes allergenic. In Italy, where it is widely eaten, it caused 25% of the mushroom poisonings recorded by the Milan poison centre between 1994 and 1999. In 2015 ANSES judged it can cause poisonings, even after canning. An order of 5 August 2016 suspended for one year the sale of fresh honey fungus without a notice about full cooking.

string-array.name: myco_craterellus_traits
string-array.item: Entirely hollow, very thin trumpet, rarely over 10 cm, with a widely wavy, scalloped margin
Inside covered in scales, grey-black to dark brown depending on moisture
Outer face almost smooth, light to dark grey: no gills, no pores
Hollow stem, the colour of the cap, tapering to the base
Pleasant fruity smell (mirabelle plum) · white spores
Broadleaf woods (beech, oak, chestnut), in groups, heavy damp soils · August to November

resources.string: The outer face is smooth: no gills. A very old, blackened russula has a convex cap and broad gills; the worthless charcoal-burner’s false chanterelle has forked gills and grows only on burnt ground. Wild mushrooms are prepared within 24 hours.

string-array.name: myco_hydnum_traits
string-array.item: Matt, more or less felted cap, whitish to ochre-brown, sometimes apricot, 3 to 10 cm; margin long rolled, then wavy
Underside covered in 3 to 6 mm spines, cream, crowded and fragile, slightly decurrent: no gills
Stocky stem, the colour of the spines, browning in places
Firm but brittle white flesh that turns orange · fruity smell, mild taste, sometimes peppery or bitter in old ones
Cream spores
Broadleaf and conifer woods, in groups, often in lines or half-circles · late summer to November

resources.string: Spines instead of gills or pores: the feature shows at once when the cap is turned over. Old specimens turn bitter.

string-array.name: myco_badia_traits
string-array.item: Chestnut to bay-brown cap, fairly uniform, 5 to 15 cm, slightly sticky when young then dry; margin rolled in young ones
Tubes whitish then greenish yellow; fine pores of the same colour that turn clearly blue when pressed or cut
Cylindrical stem, 5 to 12 cm, smooth, no net, light brown to ochre, tough with age
Whitish, firm flesh that turns a little blue above the tubes · faint smell, mild taste
Olive-brown spores
Mostly under conifers, on moss or humus, non-chalky soil · summer to autumn

resources.string: Eat only well cooked: Tox Info Suisse asks for at least 20 minutes of cooking. The bluing is not a sign of poison. No net on the stem, no red pores: otherwise it is not a bay bolete.

string-array.name: myco_chrysenteron_traits
string-array.item: Grey-brown to olive-brown cap, 3 to 8 cm, dry, quickly cracking to show pink-red flesh in the cracks
Yellow then olive-yellow tubes; wide, angular pores that hardly turn blue
Slender stem, 4 to 8 cm, yellow, ribbed or spotted with garnet red, more purplish towards the base
When cut, the lower half of the stem turns beetroot red; yellowish flesh in the stem, whitish in the cap
Olive-brown spores
All woods, summer to November

resources.string: An edible of middling quality, only cooked: pick young, firm ones and remove the stem. Its many look-alikes in the same group are told apart when cut (colour of the stem flesh), not by eye.

string-array.name: myco_erythropus_traits
string-array.item: Dark brown to chocolate-brown cap, 5 to 20 cm, dry, velvety
Yellow tubes; fine blood-red to orange-red pores that turn strongly blue when pressed
Thick stem, 5 to 15 cm, yellow under fine bright red dots: dots, not a net
Bright yellow, firm flesh that turns strongly blue when cut (the blue fades within an hour or a few) · mild taste
Olive-brown spores
Broadleaf and conifer woods, non-chalky soil · June to November

resources.string: Eat only well cooked: raw or undercooked it causes gastroenteritis, and Tox Info Suisse asks for at least 20 minutes of cooking. A stem with red dots and no net is the main feature that sets it apart from Satan’s bolete and several other toxic red boletes, whose stem has a net.

string-array.name: myco_prunulus_traits
string-array.item: White to pale grey cap, matt, as if frosted, 3 to 13 cm, dished in the centre with age; margin rolled and wavy
Decurrent gills, white then pink when ripe
Short stem, 2 to 5 cm, often off-centre and flared at the top
Soft white flesh with a strong smell of fresh flour that disappears when cooked
Pink to salmon-pink spores
Grass and woodland edges, under broadleaves or conifers · summer to autumn, a few weeks before porcini

resources.string: Toxic white clitocybes (muscarine) are sometimes mistaken for it: their gills stay white or cream and their spores are white, whereas its spores are pink. The floury smell is not enough: the livid pinkgill has it too.

string-array.name: myco_deliciosus_traits
string-array.item: Orange cap, 5 to 12 cm, with darker concentric zones, dished in the centre then funnel-shaped; margin rolled at first
Close, pale orange to yellow-orange gills
Bright orange milk, not abundant, mild, turning red very slowly and barely turning green
Short stem, 2 to 4 cm, pitted with dark orange hollows
Carrot-orange flesh that darkens; white core in the stem · fruity smell
Pale cream-yellow spores · with pines, dry warm woods · autumn

resources.string: The orange milk is the deciding feature: cut it to see it. The woolly milkcap looks like it from above, but its milk is white and it irritates the gut. If the colour of the milk has not been checked, do not conclude.

string-array.name: myco_torminosus_traits
string-array.item: Pink and ochre cap, up to 10 cm, dished in the centre, with darker zones; margin rolled, hairy in young ones
Narrow, close, flesh-coloured gills
White milk, acrid, peppery, not changing in air
Cylindrical stem, pale flesh colour, finely downy, up to 8 cm
Cream to pale yellow spores
Mostly with birches, in mixed woods

resources.string: Toxic: nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea less than 3 hours after the meal, lasting under about 12 hours (mild resinoid syndrome, per the Belgian poison centre). Its acrid milk strongly irritates the gut. The white milk sets it apart from the saffron milk cap.

string-array.name: myco_nuda_traits
string-array.item: Blue-violet to grey-violet cap, often brownish in the centre, 4 to 15 cm, smooth and moist; margin rolled
Deep violet, close gills turning dull brown with age
Stocky stem, 2 to 10 cm, lilac to grey-violet, slightly swollen at the base, with silvery fibrils
White flesh tinged violet at the top of the stem · pleasant, fruity, slightly aniseed smell
Pale pink spores
Broadleaf and conifer woods, on litter, often in rings · late season, after the first frosts

resources.string: Some violet webcaps look like it and are very toxic: their spores are rusty brown (its spores are pale pink), they often keep remnants of a cortina and their smell is unpleasant. All red, purple or orange webcaps are to be distrusted.

string-array.name: myco_orellanus_traits
string-array.item: Orange-brown to tawny cap (annatto colour), 2 to 8 cm, felted with fine fibres; margin often rolled
Widely spaced gills, ochre to reddish, then rust
Stem 4 to 9 cm, the colour of the cap or slightly paler, yellowish at the top, tapering to the base; fleeting pale yellow cortina, often absent
Pale ochre flesh, faint smell of radish when cut
Rusty brown spores
Broadleaf woods, from lowlands to mountains, fairly rare · July to December

resources.string: Deadly for the kidney, with no early warning. Digestive upset may appear 24 to 36 hours after the meal, or be missing; intense thirst, vomiting, back pain and scant urine come 2 to 20 days later. Dialysis is needed; recovery happens in 50 to 70% of cases, and kidney damage is sometimes permanent. It looks like many small brown webcaps: all red, purple or orange webcaps are to be distrusted.

string-array.name: myco_virescens_traits
string-array.item: Pale green to verdigris cap on a cream background, 5 to 12 cm, dry, cracking into small polygonal patches
Cream-white, brittle gills, sometimes spotted rusty brown
White stem, 4 to 8 cm, thick, brittle, no ring and no volva
Thick, brittle white flesh · mild, nutty taste
White spores
Broadleaf woods, warm places, edges · July to October

resources.string: The cracked, patchy cap, the flesh that snaps like chalk, and the absence of ring and volva set it apart from the death cap, which is smooth, has a ring and a volva, and whose flesh does not snap. The green form of the death cap is sometimes mistaken for a russula (Belgian poison centre).

string-array.name: myco_columbetta_traits
string-array.item: Pure white cap, sometimes cream in the centre, 4 to 10 cm, silky and shiny, slightly sticky in damp weather; conical then convex, wavy margin
Broad white gills
White stem, 6 to 14 cm, cylindrical, downy, no ring and no volva
Firm white flesh, floury smell and taste
White spores
Oaks, beeches, poor acid soils · August to November

resources.string: Everything is white, as in the destroying angel and the white form of the death cap, which are deadly: the ring and the volva, both absent here, set them apart, and the volva is underground. A pale livid pinkgill looks like it too: very fibrous cap, yellow or pink gills. Fairly rare in France.

string-array.name: myco_ostreatus_traits
string-array.item: Oyster-shell then fan-shaped cap, 7 to 14 cm, grey-brown to almost black, often much paler; thin margin, rolled at first, then scalloped
White, fairly close, forked gills that run down the stem (decurrent)
Short stem (1 to 2 cm) or almost none, lateral, white, firm
White flesh, thin except at the base of the stem, quickly elastic · mild taste
Pale spores (cream to white)
In overlapping clusters on living or dead broadleaf trees, from autumn into winter

resources.string: It grows on wood, in overlapping clusters: that is the first feature. The related oyster mushrooms (horn of plenty oyster, lung oyster) are edible too, so the confusion is harmless. The spores are allergenic for people who breathe a lot of them, such as growers.

string-array.name: myco_perlatum_traits
string-array.item: Pear-shaped, whitish body: a ball up to 6 cm wide on a sterile conical stem that makes up two thirds of the height
Surface covered in small spines and large conical warts that fall off gradually, leaving small round scars
Pure white, even, soft inside when young; yellowish, then olive-brown and powdery with age
When ripe, a round pore opens at the top to release the brown spores
Under conifers and in mixed woods, alone or in groups · summer and autumn

resources.string: Only when young, with pure white, even, soft flesh inside. Cut it in two lengthwise: a mushroom already formed inside gives away an amanita egg, which is deadly. Amanita eggs usually have no spines or warts. Spores breathed in can badly irritate the lungs.

string-array.name: myco_egg_traits
string-array.item: When young, a white egg wrapped in the universal veil
Smooth surface, no spines or warts
Cut in two lengthwise: the cap and stem are already formed, enclosed in a thick sac
Later: pale green, yellow-green or olive-green cap, ring, sac-like volva
The young, egg-shaped forms can be mistaken for puffballs

resources.string: A single mushroom is enough to cause serious poisoning: the amatoxins destroy the liver, and the signs come late, over 6 hours after the meal. Cut the egg in two lengthwise before concluding anything: a puffball is white and solid all through, an amanita egg already shows the mushroom.

string-array.name: myco_citrinum_traits
string-array.item: Irregular ball, often flattened at the poles, 2 to 12 cm, almost no stem, fixed to the ground by mycelial cords
Very thick skin (1 to 5 mm), ochre yellow with brown scales, cracking into pyramidal warts
Dense inside, pale grey at first, then violet-black marbled with white, powdery at the end
Unpleasant, sour smell (old onions, rubber)
No clear opening at the top: the skin tears at maturity
Dark olive-brown spores · acid soils, under broadleaves or conifers · late summer and autumn

resources.string: Toxic: a pharmacy thesis from Angers on 134 cases recorded by the French poison centres between 2000 and 2022 reports digestive upset and, sometimes severely, unusual heart and nervous-system signs. It is mistaken for a puffball: a puffball is pure white and even inside, not grey then black. It tears open at maturity instead of opening by a pore.

string-array.name: myco_pardinum_traits
string-array.item: Silvery grey cap, 6 to 10 cm (up to 20), covered in dark scales in circles, grey to blackish towards the centre; margin rolled at first
Almost free, close, thick gills, cream-white or greyish, sometimes yellowish; they may weep
Thick stem, 3 to 8 cm, white to pale grey or brownish, thicker at the base, no ring and no volva; the base browns or yellows when pressed
Firm, whitish flesh, floury smell and taste
White spores
Chalky soil, often near beeches or firs, at altitude, often alone · summer and autumn

resources.string: Toxic, even in small amounts: nausea, violent vomiting and diarrhoea within three hours, lasting 24 to 48 hours, sometimes with a bitter mouth, salivation or a dry mouth (severe resinoid syndrome, per the Belgian poison centre). The grey knight, smaller, darker and without scales, looks like it.

string-array.name: myco_terreum_traits
string-array.item: Mouse-grey to dark grey cap, 4 to 8 cm, felted, with radial fibres that show the white flesh with age; pale, wavy margin
Notched, fragile, rather distant gills, whitish to pearl grey
Whitish stem, 3 to 8 cm, no ring
White to light grey flesh
White spores
Open conifer woods, mostly under pines · autumn, into winter

resources.string: Opinions differ. The German mycological society (2026), the Swiss controllers (2023) and French Wikipedia call it edible. A 2014 Chinese study found substances that damage muscle in mice, as in the yellow knight; a 2016 comment disputes it and a 2024 Italian study finds none and concludes it is edible. The most cautious status is kept: not recommended. The Swiss controllers say it is easily mistaken for the toxic tiger tricholoma and for some fibrecaps; ANSES records livid entolomas picked instead of « petits gris », the name it gives to the grey knight.

string-array.name: myco_silvicola_traits
string-array.item: White to cream cap, 6 to 9 cm (sometimes 12), globular then spreading, turning yellow with age or when touched
Close gills, pale cream, then pink, then gradually chocolate brown
Slender stem, 6 to 12 cm, whitish grey, with a bulb at the base
A single ring, very wide, descending, fragile, turning yellowish
Thin whitish flesh that yellows in the stem · mild taste, strong smell of aniseed or almond
Dark brown spores · in small groups in woods · summer and autumn

resources.string: Its gills, pale cream at first, make it mistaken for the deadly white amanitas, including the white form of the death cap. Amanitas have a volva at the base of the stem, always white gills and no aniseed smell. The German mycological society points out that yellowing agarics can concentrate a lot of cadmium.

string-array.name: myco_granulatus_traits
string-array.item: Sticky, shiny, smooth cap, up to 12 cm, yellowish beige to reddish brown, often evenly coloured
Adnate tubes, pale yellow then olive-yellow; evenly coloured pores that weep milky drops at first
Stem about 10 × 2 cm, yellowish with opalescent droplets, then yellower and dotted at the top with brown or russet granules; no ring
Yellowish-white flesh, slightly sour · spicy smell
Orange-brown spores with an olive sheen
Under pines

resources.string: Its sticky skin is laxative. ANSES attributes digestive upset to it, often with trembling, headaches and anxiety, a few hours after the meal: 25 cases recorded in France between 1999 and 2015. No cooking is shown to be effective. Skin contact can also cause dermatitis. The Swiss controllers list it among edible species while asking for the cap skin to be removed, and the German mycological society also lists it as edible: the most cautious status is kept.

Listed in several guides as a mediocre edible, although its sticky skin contains laxative substances. Its toxic power has been known since 1923. In 2015, ANSES judged that it can cause poisoning, even after canning. A decree of 5 August 2016 suspends for one year the sale of fresh granulated bolete not accompanied by information on thorough cooking.

string-array.name: myco_olivacea_traits
string-array.item: Matt, finely wrinkled cap, up to 20 cm, variable in colour, often mottled green and red
Cream gills, then ochre-yellow with glaucous reflections, then orange; edge lined with red towards the margin
Stem about 12 × 4 cm, dotted, lilac pink at least under the gills, more or less yellowing
Mild flesh · slightly fruity smell
Yellow spores
Under broadleaves, mostly beeches, in lowlands but mainly in mountains, up to 1,800 m · July to November

resources.string: Digestive poisonings are reported mostly when it is eaten raw or lightly cooked, on a barbecue for instance: in Italy, a few dozen cases a year; in the Basque Country, over 40 cases in twenty years; in France, 3 grouped cases in 2012, with vomiting 2 hours later. ANSES judged in 2015 that the risk cannot be ruled out, even after cooking; Tox Info Suisse asks for at least 20 minutes of cooking.

Sometimes eaten, and even judged edible in Eastern Europe. In 2015, ANSES judged that the risk of poisoning cannot be ruled out, even after cooking, for lack of data proving it harmless. A decree of 5 August 2016 suspends for one year the sale of fresh olive brittlegill not accompanied by information on thorough cooking.

string-array.name: myco_ovoidea_traits
string-array.item: White to very pale grey cap, thick, 15 to 20 cm (up to 30), hemispherical at first, flaky; the margin often keeps hanging cottony scraps of the veil
White, close, broad, free gills that may turn slightly pink with age
White, stout, powdery stem, 15 to 20 cm
Cream, fragile, cottony ring that tends to disappear
Large sac-like volva at the base, white to ochre-beige
Thick white flesh, strong unpleasant smell · white spores
Under broadleaves and especially pines, on sunny limy soil, in summer and autumn; fairly common in the south of France

resources.string: Not recommended: books call it edible in some places and poisonous in others, and it is on neither the German mycological society list of edible species (2026) nor the Swiss controllers’ list (2023). ANSES records it among the mushrooms picked instead of puffballs or boletes in the second half of 2022. Its look-alike, Amanita proxima, damages the kidneys; poisonings happened in the south of France when it was mistaken for the bearded amanita: more russet volva, ring that stays, smooth margin.

string-array.name: myco_geotropa_traits
string-array.item: Cap 7 to 20 cm, cream, buff to cinnamon-brown: keel-shaped when young, then domed, then spreading with a boss, finally funnel-shaped; smooth margin
Fine, deeply decurrent gills, cream to buff
Solid, fibrous stem, 10 to 20 cm, very swollen when young, the colour of the cap; no ring
White flesh, firm when young · strong, sweet smell of bitter almond or hay
White spores
On the ground in broadleaf woods, edges and clearings, often in troops or rings, from late summer until the first frosts

resources.string: Edible of middling value, only when young: the fibrous stem becomes tough and is thrown away. It is on the German mycological society list (« Mönchskopf ») and on the Swiss controllers’ list (« tête de moine »). ANSES records livid entolomas picked instead of trooping funnels (2022): the entoloma has notched gills that turn pink, a floury smell and pink spores. The miller, also edible, has pink spores.

string-array.name: myco_amethystina_traits
string-array.item: Cap 2 to 8 cm, dark violet, matt, convex then dished like a navel; it fades and whitens as it dries; thin, striate margin
Gills the colour of the cap, distant, unequal
Stem 4 to 10 cm, slender and twisted, the colour of the cap, downy towards the base, fibrous
Thin, pale lilac flesh, mild smell and taste
White spores
Damp woods of broadleaves or conifers, from late summer to early winter

resources.string: Edible: it is on the German mycological society list and on the Swiss controllers’ list; the fibrous stem is not eaten. On polluted soil it can accumulate arsenic compounds: the German society advises against picking it near former military grounds, mines, factories and busy roads. The lilac bonnet, which is toxic, looks like it: ANSES records mycenas picked instead of deceivers.

string-array.name: myco_pura_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 7 cm, convex without being pointed, then spreading with a slight boss; from pure pink to violet or grey, it whitens in dry weather; very thin margin, striate from the gills
Unequal, fairly distant gills, whitish to pinkish
Stem 4 to 9 cm, the colour of the cap or more violet, slightly striate, fragile, hollow
White flesh · clear smell and taste of radish
White spores
Common from spring to autumn, under broadleaves and conifers

resources.string: Toxic: it contains muscarine, which causes the sweating syndrome: heavy sweating, tears and salivation, short breath, nausea and vomiting, within minutes to 2 hours (Belgian poison centre). The German mycological society lists Mycena pura and Mycena rosea among muscarine mushrooms; M. rosea is often only a variety of M. pura. In 2022, pickers looking for amethyst deceivers picked mycenas (ANSES). The deceiver has more distant gills, a hard stem and no smell of radish.

string-array.name: myco_calopus_traits
string-array.item: Cap about 15 cm (rarely 20), white, beige to olive, smooth or finely hairy, sometimes cracked with age
Fine, pale yellow pores that turn blue when touched then olive; tubes up to 2 cm
Stem 7 to 15 cm by 2 to 5, yellow above, red below, sometimes all reddish, with a raised white net at the top; the red may fade with age
Thick, firm, whitish to pale yellow flesh that turns blue when cut · bitter taste
Olive to olive-brown spores
Under broadleaves and conifers, mostly beeches and oaks, often at altitude, on chalky soil · July to December

resources.string: Toxic: the German mycological society list puts it among the gastrointestinal-syndrome mushrooms. The bitterness does not go away with cooking and it can cause vomiting. ANSES records scarlet-stemmed boletes picked instead of dotted-stem boletes (2022) and the Zurich laboratory sorts it out among the toxic boletes (2023). It has the red stem of Satan’s bolete, but yellow pores; the porcino has no red stem.

string-array.name: myco_brunneum_traits
string-array.item: Cap 6 to 15 cm, stout, globular then flat, no boss; broken into whitish, beige or brown plates or scales, often star-like; only the centre stays smooth
Free, broad gills, dirty ochre-white then pinkish cream
Stem 6 to 15 cm, white then ochre, smooth, turning saffron red when scraped; large bulb with a sharp edge, often off-centre
Thick but single, sliding ring
Thick white flesh that quickly reddens when cut then browns · mild taste
White spores
Gardens, parks, compost heaps, greenhouses and nitrogen-rich soils, near houses

resources.string: Toxic: digestive upset, rarely serious, varying with the person and the quantity; the German mycological society list puts it among the gastrointestinal-syndrome mushrooms. Wikipedia counts it among the mushrooms that cause the most poisonings each year, often mistaken for the parasol; ANSES records it among the 2022 confusions. The Swiss controllers point out that it looks like Chlorophyllum rhacodes (shaggy parasol), which is edible.

string-array.name: myco_rhacodes_traits
string-array.item: Cap 8 to 18 cm, egg-shaped then almost flat, grey-beige to ochre-brown, covered in woolly, curled tufts of dull brown; only the centre stays smooth
White, very close gills that redden when touched
Stem 10 to 20 cm, smooth, hollow, grey, bulbous
Double, thick, sliding, smooth, whitish ring
Thick, tender white flesh · mild taste; the whole mushroom turns bright red and saffron when cut or scraped, then browns
White spores
Soil of broadleaf and conifer woods and of meadows at the edge, from late summer to autumn

resources.string: A good edible according to Wikipedia, except the stem, which is fibrous and tough. Some people get gastroenteritis, which the article blames on the nitrates of very rich soils; others are allergic. The German mycological society and Swiss controllers’ lists put it among the edible species, under the name Chlorophyllum olivieri. Do not mistake it for Chlorophyllum brunneum (sharp-edged bulb, single ring, toxic), nor for the deadly parasol, which is much smaller.

string-array.name: myco_emetica_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 10 cm, bright cherry red, sticky; convex then spreading and slightly dished; the skin peels almost to the centre
White to cream, close, broad, adnate gills
White stem, 5 to 9 cm, sometimes swollen at the base; no ring
White flesh, pinkish under the skin, brittle · faintly fruity smell
White spores
Sandy soils, among mosses and sphagnum, mostly under conifers and pines · July to October

resources.string: Toxic: digestive upset, mostly vomiting, between half an hour and three hours after the meal; it usually passes by itself (Wikipedia EN). The German mycological society lists the Russula emetica group among the gastrointestinal-syndrome mushrooms, and the Belgian poison centre cites the sickener among the causes of the mild resinoid syndrome (under 12 hours). Many red russulas look alike and some can only be told apart under a microscope: the cap is not enough.

string-array.name: myco_cyanoxantha_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 12 cm (up to 15), convex then flattened and dished; very variable colours, often mixed: greenish black, violet grey, blue green, lilac, pink, ochre, yellow, green
White then pale cream, often forked gills, flexible and greasy to the touch: they bend without breaking
White stem, 5 to 10 cm, solid to stuffed; no ring
White flesh · mild taste, reminiscent of hazelnut
White spores
Under broadleaves and conifers, mostly beeches and spruces, from early summer to late autumn

resources.string: An excellent edible according to Wikipedia, on the German mycological society and Swiss controllers’ lists. Its mark: flexible, greasy gills that bend without breaking, whereas other russulas have brittle gills. Many russulas look alike, and the German society puts acrid and bitter russulas among the gastrointestinal-syndrome mushrooms; ANSES records pickers of charcoal burners who picked another russula (2022). A russula has neither ring nor volva, unlike the death cap.

string-array.name: myco_hebeloma_traits
string-array.item: Cap 5 to 10 cm, convex then spreading, with a central boss; whitish ochre to reddish, paler at the margin; sticky in damp weather
Fairly close, toothed gills, whitish then brown; in damp weather they weep brownish drops
Stem 5 to 10 cm, whitish, rust-stained towards the base, slightly swollen below, frosted over a good length; no ring
Fairly thick white flesh · distinct smell of radish, bitter taste
Ochre to brown spores
Fairly common in summer and autumn, under broadleaves or conifers, in groups along paths and ditches, in lawns

resources.string: Toxic: digestive upset, from mild to marked (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, cramps) (Wikipedia EN). The German mycological society lists the whole Hebeloma genus among the gastrointestinal-syndrome mushrooms, and the Belgian poison centre cites the poison pie among the causes of the mild resinoid syndrome: moderate gastroenteritis, less than 3 hours after the meal, lasting under 12 hours. The risk is confusion with tricholomas (Wikipedia FR): the radish smell and the browning gills help to recognise it.

string-array.name: myco_aegerita_traits
string-array.item: Fleshy cap 3 to 10 cm, convex then flat, smooth and silky, tawny brown when young then beige to pale ochre, lighter towards the margin; slightly cracked towards the centre
Close, pale beige then brownish, adnate gills
Firm, fibrous, solid stem, pale then reddish brown, often curved
Ample, membranous, white, persistent ring; it turns tobacco-coloured under the falling spores
Whitish flesh · hazelnut taste, strong fruity smell of old cask
Dirty brown spores
In tufts at the foot of trees and on dead wood, mostly poplars and willows, in autumn

resources.string: A very good edible according to Wikipedia FR; the German mycological society and Swiss controllers’ lists put it under the name Cyclocybe cylindracea (« pholiote du peuplier »). Wikipedia EN warns that it resembles some deadly species, without naming them, and that the genus is difficult to identify.

string-array.name: myco_tubaeformis_traits
string-array.item: Cap 3 to 7 cm, convex then dished into a funnel, often pierced at the centre onto the hollow stem; brown to tawny, greyish; margin rolled when young then wavy
No true gills underneath: grey or silvery-yellow folds, branched and forked near the edge, running down the stem
Stem 3 to 12 cm, bright yellow, long, thin, winding and hollow
Thin, yellowish flesh, faint smell
Pale spores (cream to pale orange-pink)
In groups, often in lines, in broadleaf or mixed woods, on moss and litter, near very rotten wood · mid-autumn to the first frosts

resources.string: A renowned edible, fresh or dried; it is on the German mycological society list (« Trompeten-Pfifferling ») and on the Swiss controllers’ list. It has edible look-alikes (Craterellus lutescens, C. melanoxeros); Leotia lubrica, gelatinous and said to be suspect, can grow alongside (Wikipedia FR).

string-array.name: myco_gigantea_traits
string-array.item: White ball without a stem, 10 to 50 cm (up to 80), which can exceed a football
Pure white, even inside when young; yellowish or greenish brown with age
When young, smell of fresh flour
White spores when young, olive when ripe
Meadows rich in droppings of ruminants or birds, sometimes in groups, broadleaf woods · late summer and autumn

resources.string: Only when young, with pure white, even flesh inside: yellowish or greenish brown, it can cause digestive upset (Wikipedia EN), and it rots within weeks. It is on the German mycological society list and on the Swiss controllers’ list. Wikipedia FR says it can fix heavy metals such as mercury: not in large quantities. Cut it in two: a young amanita egg already shows the future cap and stem; throw it away and wash the knife.
